instrument: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030)
description: Outlines seven clear targets and four priorities for action to prevent new and reduce existing disaster risks. Aims to substantially reduce disaster risk and losses in lives, livelihoods, and health.
governanceRole:
Multisectoral Collaboration (Priority 2): Emphasizes strengthening disaster risk governance across sectors, promoting coordination essential for One Health approaches
Health System Resilience (Para 30i): Calls for enhancing cooperation between health authorities and other stakeholders to strengthen country capacity for disaster risk management and implementation of the International Health Regulations
Ecosystem Approach (Para 30n): Promotes sustainable use and management of ecosystems, aligning with One Health's emphasis on environmental health
Zoonotic Disease Focus (WHO Director-General Statement, 2020): Recognizes the need for a One Health approach in addressing zoonotic diseases and implementing the Sendai Framework
limitations:
Limited Health Integration (Midterm Review, 2023): Despite health mentions, the primary emphasis remains on disaster risk reduction, potentially overlooking some aspects of the One Health approach
Implementation Challenges (Midterm Review, 2023): Ongoing difficulties in fully implementing the framework, particularly in developing countries, may hinder comprehensive One Health strategies
Fragmented Governance (Midterm Review, 2023): Despite promoting a whole-of-society approach, challenges remain in coordinating across sectors and levels of government, potentially hindering One Health implementation
provisions:
Paragraph 15 – All-Hazards Scope: Broadens the definition of disasters to include biological hazards. The Framework explicitly acknowledges that factors like climate change, ecosystem decline, pandemics and epidemics heighten disaster risk

Priority 3, ¶30(i) – Resilient Health Systems: Calls on countries to “enhance the resilience of national health systems, including by integrating disaster risk management into primary, secondary and tertiary health care”

Priority 2 & 4, e.g. ¶31(e) – Coherence with IHR and One Health: Emphasizes coordination across sectors and with international health regulations. Countries are encouraged to strengthen cooperation between disaster risk agencies and health authorities, including implementation of the International Health Regulations (2005) as part of disaster preparedness
interlinkages: International Health Regulations

instrument: WHO Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance
description: Provides a framework for national action to combat antimicrobial resistance, with the main goal of ensuring treatment and prevention of infectious diseases with quality-assured, safe and effective medicines. Emphasizes the One Health approach, addressing the use of antimicrobials in human health, animal health, and agriculture in its newest update.
governanceRole:
Multisectoral Collaboration (Strategic Objective 2): Promotes a One Health approach by emphasizing cooperation between human health, animal health, and environmental sectors to combat AMR; overall plan being updated to align with One Health guiding principle
Capacity Building (Strategic Objective 3): Focuses on strengthening knowledge through surveillance and research, supporting countries in developing One Health-aligned AMR monitoring systems
Implementation Framework (Strategic Objective 5): Provides a blueprint for countries to develop and implement multisectoral National Action Plans on AMR
Global Governance (Strategic Objective 1): Establishes a framework for global coordination, including the Quadripartite collaboration, facilitating a unified One Health approach to AMR
limitations:
Implementation Challenges (TrACSS 2022): Only 24% of countries report effective implementation of their National Action Plans, hindering comprehensive AMR strategies
Resource Constraints (TrACSS 2022): Only 10% of countries report allocating dedicated financing for AMR initiatives, limiting the capacity to implement One Health approaches
Fragmented Governance (TrACSS 2022): 51% of countries report that their multisectoral coordination mechanisms are not functional, impeding effective One Health collaboration
Limited Environmental Focus (Comprehensive Review, 2021): Despite the One Health approach, the environmental dimension of AMR remains underrepresented in many National Action Plans
provisions:
One Health Approach: The Global AMR Plan “underscores the need for an effective ‘One Health’ approach” involving coordination among human health, veterinary, agriculture, environment and other sectors

Strategic Objective 4 – Optimize Antimicrobial Use: A key objective is “to optimize the use of antimicrobial medicines in human and animal health”​

Multisectoral Collaboration: The plan calls for strong collaboration with FAO and OIE, and for all countries to have national One Health AMR action plans by 2017. It pushes for integrated surveillance of AMR across human clinical settings, farms, and food chains, and for public awareness campaigns targeting both healthcare providers and farmers
interlinkages:
Code of Practice to Minimize and Contain Foodborne Antimicrobial Resistance (CXC 61-2005)
Guidelines for Risk Analysis of Foodborne Antimicrobial Resistance (CXG 77-2011)
Guidelines on Integrated Monitoring and Surveillance of Foodborne Antimicrobial Resistance (CXG 94-2021)
WOAH Strategy on Antimicrobial Resistance

instrument: WOAH Strategy on Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR)
description: Supports WOAH Members to confront the shared global threat of AMR in animals and humans. The standards and guidelines provide a framework for responsible and prudent use of antimicrobial products in animals, and for surveillance of use of antimicrobials and antimicrobial resistance. The communication and advocacy materials foster understanding of the risks of AMR and encourage the adoption of measures that slow its spread.
governanceRole:
Cooperation and information sharing: Facilitates international cooperation and information sharing on AMR
Promotion of responsible antimicrobial stewardship: Advocates for reduced and more targeted antimicrobial use in veterinary medicine, directly benefiting both public health and ecosystems
Integration of environmental dimensions in AMR control: Recognizes the role of environmental contamination in the spread of resistance genes
limitations:
Implementation: Challenges due to varying resources among member countries
Gaps in environmental surveillance and regulation: While acknowledging environmental risks, implementation of AMR monitoring in ecosystems (e.g., wastewater, wildlife reservoirs) remains underdeveloped
provisions:
Awareness and Education: Emphasizes the importance of global awareness campaigns and educational initiatives to inform stakeholders across human, animal, and environmental health sectors about the risks of AMR and the need for responsible antimicrobial use

Surveillance and Research: Advocates for the development and enhancement of integrated surveillance systems to monitor antimicrobial use and resistance patterns across humans, animals, and the environment

Good Governance and Capacity Building: Encourages strengthening national and international regulatory frameworks and building capacities within veterinary and public health services to implement effective AMR strategies
interlinkages:
Code of Practice to Minimize and Contain Foodborne Antimicrobial Resistance (CXC 61-2005)
Guidelines for Risk Analysis of Foodborne Antimicrobial Resistance (CXG 77-2011)
Guidelines on Integrated Monitoring and Surveillance of Foodborne Antimicrobial Resistance
WHO global action plan on antimicrobial resistance

instrument: WHA 72(9) WHO global strategy on health, environment and climate change
description: Notes the WHO Global Strategy, which sets a transformative agenda to reduce the 13 million annual deaths linked to environmental factors by 2030. The strategy calls for a shift toward primary prevention and cross-sectoral policy integration, urging governments and the health sector to act on upstream environmental determinants of health—such as air pollution, climate change, water and sanitation, and chemical safety. It emphasizes environmental justice, sustainable governance, and the central role of the health sector in driving intersectoral action, backed by evidence, monitoring, and public accountability.
governanceRole:
Mainstreams environmental health into public health leadership: Empowers the health sector to take an upstream role in environmental decision-making, enabling more integrated governance over land use, food systems, energy, and urban development
Creates formal platforms for cross-sectoral coordination: Calls for new or strengthened governance mechanisms, such as “Health in All Policies” and intersectoral bodies, that embed One Health principles into law and national planning processes.
Promotes integrated surveillance of environmental, animal, and human health risks: By encouraging linked environmental monitoring and public health surveillance, the strategy supports early warning systems that can detect and respond to threats across sectors.
limitations:
One Health framing is present but underdeveloped operationally: Although the strategy invokes One Health and “Health in All Policies,” it does not establish joint implementation plans or institutional accountability mechanisms across sectors.
Environmental partners are tasked with implementation but not co-governance: While the strategy calls on environmental sectors to act, it does not create shared governance platforms or co-leadership structures, potentially reinforcing imbalanced ownership of One Health goals.
provisions:
Strategic Objective 1, pg. 8: Adoption of a One Health approach, a holistic, cross-sectoral and multidisciplinary approach, is to be sought where appropriate, for example to address antimicrobial resistance

Strategic Objective 4, pg. 11: Efficient and overarching governance mechanisms can decisively facilitate cross-sectoral work… More holistic approaches and the protection of goods for health, such as clean air or a stable climate, are aimed for, in coordination with the health sector.

Strategic Objective 5, pg. 15: Capacity must be built… for targeted environmental monitoring linked to public health surveillance… including linked surveillance of pathogens in wildlife and human beings, in order to lower risk and increase preparedness for health threats resulting from human influence on natural ecosystems
interlinkages:
UNFCCC
Paris Agreement
Global Action Plan on Climate Change and Health (A78/27)

instrument: Codex Code of Practice to Minimize and Contain Foodborne AMR (CXC 61-2005, revised 2021)
description: The Codex Alimentarius is a collection of internationally adopted food standards and related texts. This code is part of a larger sub-compendium of Codex texts intended to support governments in designing and running a successful strategy to tackle foodborne AMR. The Code of Practice addresses the responsible and prudent use of antimicrobial agents by participants in the food chain, including competent authorities, the pharmaceutical industry, veterinarians, and plant/crop health professionals, and food producers and processors. It provides guidance on measures and practices at from production to retail of food to prevent, minimize and contain foodborne AMR in the food supply.
governanceRole:
Cross-Sectoral Implementation: Requiring cross-sectoral coordination and harmonized policies on AMR. It involves stakeholders from the veterinary sector, agriculture (food producers), public health, and even the pharmaceutical industry in implementation​.
National plans: Prompts countries to incorporate guidance into national AMR action plans, inherently One Health platforms (bringing together human health, animal health, agriculture, and environment authorities).
Surveillance: Promotes integrated surveillance of AMR in food, animals, and humans, thereby fostering data-sharing and collaboration among sectors.
limitations:
Scope challenges: While the code addresses AMR in food production, effective One Health governance requires concurrent actions in human healthcare and environmental sectors which are outside Codex’s scope; the code’s impact depends on other sectors (e.g. human medicine stewardship, wastewater management) also doing their part.
Implementation capacity: Implementation in low-resource settings may be hindered by lack of capacity (e.g. to control over-the-counter antibiotic sales for animals or to monitor compliance). Without strong political commitment, the recommended practices may not be fully adopted, weakening the One Health response to AMR.
provisions:
General Principles 1-4, 6, 16: Specifically mentions that One Health approaches sensitive to should be taken when determining AMR risk management priorities, and best practices from human, animal, and plant health should be reflected in priorities and decision-making.

Section 5 - Responsible and Prudent Use of Antimicrobial Agents: National governments should collaborate with professionals across plant, animal, and human health-related sectors to promote responsible and prudent use of antimicrobial agents along the food chain.

Section 7 - Consumer Practices and Communication to Consumers: Risk communication to consumers should be sensitive to local knowledge and utilize best practices from WHO, FAO, OIE, and One Health AMR resources.
interlinkages:
WTO SPS Agreement
WHO Global Action Plan on AMR
WOAH AMR Strategy

instrument: Codex General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995, Revised 2023)
description: The Codex Alimentarius is a collection of internationally adopted food standards and related texts. This code is part of a larger sub-compendium of Codex texts intended to support governments in designing and running a successful strategy to tackle foodborne AMR. This Codex standard that sets out the general principles for managing chemical contaminants in foods and animal feeds and provides a list of maximum levels (MLs) for many important contaminants and natural toxins. Its scope includes environmental contaminants (like heavy metals), naturally occurring toxins (like mycotoxins), and other unintended chemicals in food/feed. Aims to protect public health and ensure fair trade by keeping contaminant levels in food and feed as low as reasonably achievable​.
governanceRole:
Collaboration: Among food safety, agriculture, and environmental authorities. For example, to enforce heavy metal limits in food, governments may need to control environmental emissions and ensure farms are not in polluted areas – linking environment ministries with food regulators. The standard’s joint focus on food and feed means veterinary and food agencies must coordinate (e.g. preventing mycotoxin-contaminated feed from reaching animals).
Facilitates trade and information exchange: Provides a unified framework that countries use to harmonize their contaminant limits, facilitating global trade and information exchange on contamination incidents. Harmonization encourages countries to develop coherent policies across sectors (such as agricultural practices, food processing, and waste management) to meet the safety benchmarks.
limitations:
Need for extensive monitoring and inter-sector cooperation: Detection and control of contaminants requires environmental monitoring (for pollutants in water, soil), agricultural interventions (good practices to prevent mold toxins or uptake of pollutants by crops), and food inspection. If environmental regulations are weak, contaminants may continue to enter the food chain, undermining the standard.
Gap of scope: Doesn’t cover pesticide residues or veterinary drugs (handled by other Codex standards)​, which means countries must integrate multiple standards – potential silos in these areas might complicate a truly One Health approach.
Resource limitations: in testing for a wide array of contaminants in both food and feed also pose difficulties for low-resource settings.
provisions:
Section 1.3: Scope – Applies to contaminants in food and feed that impact human health, including heavy metals and mycotoxins.

Section 3: Maximum Levels (MLs) – Establishes limits for contaminants like lead, aflatoxins, and mercury to prevent toxic exposures.
interlinkages: WTO SPS Agreement

instrument: General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969, Revised 2022)
description: The Codex Alimentarius is a collection of internationally adopted food standards and related texts. The principles are part of a larger sub-compendium of Codex texts intended to support governments in designing and running a successful strategy to tackle foodborne AMR. It provides a foundational code of practice on food hygiene applicable “throughout the food processing, manufacture, and marketing chain” to prevent food contamination. Establishes Good Hygiene Practices (GHPs) and a Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) system as a framework to ensure food is safe and suitable for consumption
governanceRole:
Cross-sectoral: Engages food producers, veterinary professionals, and regulators in a unified hygiene framework, thereby requiring communication between agriculture (on-farm practices) and public health authorities.
Trading benefits: The standard’s international adoption harmonizes food safety measures, enabling countries to work together to protect health and maintain confidence in traded food​
limitations:
Siloes: The code primarily focuses on food production and handling; engaging environmental authorities or addressing broader ecological contexts (beyond hygiene of water and waste) is not explicit. In countries with fragmented responsibilities, ensuring cooperation between veterinary services, food safety authorities, and environmental agencies can be difficult.
Capacity concerns: Limited resources or expertise (e.g. for conducting HACCP in small farms) may inhibit full application, potentially creating gaps in the One Health continuum. Moreover, the code’s broad nature requires adaptation to specific contexts, which, if not done with multi-sector input, could limit its One Health effectiveness.
provisions:
Section 3: Primary Production – Requires control of contamination from soil, water, feed, fertilizers, and veterinary drugs to prevent zoonotic hazards.

Section 5: Control of Operation – Mandates HACCP-based controls to prevent foodborne contamination and ensure hygiene throughout the food chain.
interlinkages: WTO SPS Agreement

instrument: Decision 15/4: Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
description: The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) is the post-2020 global biodiversity strategy to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. It sets 4 global goals and 23 targets, integrating biodiversity into all sectors. The GBF explicitly embeds biodiversity-health interlinkages and the One Health approach, among other holistic approaches, as cross-cutting implementation principles.
governanceRole:
Elevates biodiversity-health linkages as a global principle: One Health is explicitly mentioned in Section C(r), with guidance for implementation through Targets 4–8 and 11.
Integrates biodiversity-health into spatial planning, food systems, and pollution governance: The GBF targets operationalize co-benefits across land use, species management, and pollution (Targets 1–8).
Anchors equity, transparency, and inclusive participation: Grounded in the right to health and environmental justice (C(g), Targets 21–23).
limitations:
No standalone One Health indicator: Implementation of One Health depends on interpretation within national biodiversity strategies.
Health ministries and systems are not explicitly included in governance mandates: Coordination depends on voluntary cross-sectoral action without institutional mandates.
provisions:
Decision §1: Formally adopts the Kunming–Montreal GBF

Section C(r): Recognizes One Health and biodiversity-health interlinkages as implementation principles.

Goal B & Target 11: Elevates ecosystem services, disease risk reduction, and nature-based solutions.

Targets 4–7: Address zoonotic risk, wildlife use, invasive species, and pollution as cross-sector threats.

Targets 14 & 21–23: Establish enabling conditions for cross-sector coordination and data sharing
interlinkages:
UN Convention on Biological Diversity
CBD Decision 16/19 (Biodiversity & Health)

instrument: One Health Joint Plan of Action
description: Joint strategy developed by the Quadripartite organizations to guide One Health implementation globally. It proposes six interdependent action tracks addressing zoonoses, AMR, food safety, environmental degradation, and endemic disease burdens. The strategy aims to operationalize and set the standard for One Health implementation through coordinated policy and capacity-building over five years.
governanceRole:
Anchors a global, shared implementation structure: The defined architecture involves the Quadripartite Executive Boards, regional coordination bodies, national implementation partnerships, and the advisory support of OHHLEP.
Provides a roadmap and operational tools for national adoption: Includes action timelines, workforce plans, surveillance integration, and legal frameworks
Defines Theory of Change and impact metrics: Clear pathways from policy, science, and implementation to system-wide change
Robust M&E Framework: Includes indicators and outcomes for all six action tracks, with alignment to the SDGs, and links to UN Sustainable Development Frameworks at country level
limitations: Limited uptake: At present, no countries in North America, South America, and Oceania have developed One Health strategic plans under the JPA, and a majority of countries in Europe, aside from France, and Asia, except for a cluster of Southeast Asian countries, have not developed strategic plans.
provisions:
Part 2 – Theory of Change and Operational Objectives: Three strategic pathways (policy/legal, organizational, data); medium-term outcomes and long-term impacts (e.g., reduced risk at the human-animal-environment interface)

Part 3 – Six Action Tracks: Each track has specific high-level actions and deliverables (e.g., Action 1.1: Legal and workforce capacity; Action 6.1: Ecosystem protection)

Part 4 – Governance and M&E: Clear roles for the Quadripartite Secretariat, OHHLEP, and regional coordination platforms; monitoring aligned with SDG contributions and national workplan

Part 5 – Resource Mobilization: Joint strategy for sustainable financing, targeting trust funds and donor alignment for LMIC implementation support

instrument: MRLs and Risk Management Recommendations for Residues of Veterinary Drugs in Foods (CXM 2-2023)
description: Compendium of standards for chemical residues in food from veterinary drugs. It lists the maximum residue limits (MRLs) – the highest levels of specific veterinary drug residues permitted in foods (meat, milk, eggs, etc.) – that are considered safe for consumers, based on scientific risk assessments. It also includes risk management recommendations (RMRs) for certain drugs (e.g. when no safe level can be determined). Helps countries regulate veterinary drug use and ensure that animal-derived foods are chemically safe for human consumption.
governanceRole:
Harmonized international benchmark: encourages regulatory cooperation. Food safety authorities and veterinary drug regulators must work together – the former rely on the standard to set national residue limits and testing programs, while the latter control drug use on farms to meet those limits.
Surveillance and testing: Coordination (often through national residue control plans) is a One Health governance success, requiring joint surveillance, data sharing, and cross-agency enforcement. The Codex MRL list, developed with global scientific input (JECFA evaluations), helps countries align their policies, thus smoothing trade and encouraging all countries to build capacity for residue monitoring and laboratory testing.
limitations:
Capacity and regulatory: Countries with limited laboratory or monitoring capacity may struggle to enforce MRLs, leading to gaps in consumer protection and animal drug oversight. Another challenge is ensuring veterinary and food safety authorities coordinate effectively – if veterinary services do not enforce prudent use or if farmers are unaware of withdrawal requirements, residues can still end up in food above the limits.
Focus on consumers: focuses on consumer health; it does not directly address environmental residues or occupational exposure, which means additional measures (outside Codex) are needed to fully protect ecosystems and farm workers.
Finite list: Codex MRLs exist for a finite list of drugs – national authorities must manage risks from veterinary chemicals not yet evaluated by Codex, which can complicate a unified One Health strategy.
provisions:
Section 2: Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) – Defines limits for veterinary drug residues in food to ensure consumer safety.

Annex: Risk Management Recommendations – Lists drugs prohibited in food-producing animals due to human health risks.
interlinkages: WTO SPS Agreement

instrument: Decision 16/19: Global Action Plan for Biodiversity and Health
description: Adopts the Global Action Plan on Biodiversity and Health, supporting the implementation of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It recognizes biodiversity as a determinant of health, supports One Health among other multisectoral approaches, and outlines voluntary actions for Parties to integrate biodiversity–health interlinkages into national strategies, with a focus on equity and multisectoral governance.
governanceRole:
Operationalizes biodiversity-health linkages across 8 GBF targets: The Action Plan provides clear guidance on how to embed One Health into land use, species management, pollution control, and AMR governance (Annex §§13)
Formalizes One Health governance structures: Calls for national focal points, interministerial coordination, and cross-sector assessment tools (Annex §§12d, 12g, 12j)
Promotes inclusive implementation: Includes gender, Indigenous peoples, youth, and persons with disabilities in policy design and monitoring (Annex §§12e, 12f).
limitations:
Resource and capacity gaps not fully mitigated: While funding is encouraged, no earmarked mechanisms exist under this decision (Decision §7, Annex §4)
Limited integration with public health system mandates: While the Action Plan bridges sectors, few specific mandates are assigned to ensure reporting (Decision §§6–9)
provisions:
Decision §1: Adopts the Global Action Plan on Biodiversity and Health as a voluntary tool aligned with the GBF.

Decision §3(a–d): Encourages national implementation, coordination, focal point designation, youth participation, and policy mainstreaming.

Annex §12: Lists general actions for biodiversity–health integration across governance, policy, education, surveillance, and inclusive participation.

Annex §13: Aligns One Health implementation actions with GBF Targets 1–8, across land use, species management, invasive species, pollution, and climate
interlinkages:
Convention on Biological Diversity
Kunming-Montreal GBF

instrument: Provisional Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Sustainable Management of Plastics in Agriculture
description: Provides guiding principles and measures that governments, manufacturers, and other agrifood system stakeholders may adopt to promote sustainable management practices for plastics used in agriculture. It covers all agricultural sub-sectors, including crops, livestock, fisheries, aquaculture, and forestry, and addresses the full lifecycle of plastics from design and manufacture through to end-of-life management. The Code is organized around seven interconnected goals, including contributing to food security, reducing plastic use that poses risks to the environment or human health, promoting sustainable product design, eliminating leakage into the environment, and supporting equitable participation of affected populations, including smallholder farmers, women, youth, and Indigenous Peoples.
governanceRole:
Establishes a cross-sectoral policy framework linking agricultural plastic management to human, animal, and environmental health. Objectives explicitly include protecting human and animal health, food safety, soil, and water from agricultural plastic pollution, providing a governance basis for addressing a diffuse, multi-pathway environmental health risk.
Promotes evidence-building and monitoring to guide decision-making: Countries are encouraged to develop strategies to measure and monitor plastics use and alternatives, and to cooperate on common data collection and reporting approaches, including relevant SDG indicators.
Supports national policy development and technical cooperation: FAO commits to developing specific technical guidelines and manuals to support implementation, and encourages countries to build their own regulatory frameworks with particular support to developing countries, economies in transition, and Small Island Developing States.
limitations:
Relationship to a future legally binding instrument: The VCoC was developed in parallel with negotiations for an international legally binding instrument on plastic pollution (INC process); it is intended to complement, not preempt, that process, and its scope and status may evolve depending on the outcome of those negotiations.
Non-binding monitoring: Countries are invited to monitor implementation and report to FAO on a voluntary basis only, with no formal compliance or review mechanism established.
provisions:
Article 2.1(ii) – Objectives: States that the VCoC aims to protect human and animal health, food safety, food security, soil, water, and the environment from pollution resulting from the use of plastics in agriculture.

Article 4.6.1(iv) – Research and Development: Calls on stakeholders to examine the pathways and impacts of plastics used in agriculture, including microplastics, on agroecosystems, food safety, and human health.

Article 5.2.2 – Alternatives Assessment: Requires that alternative practices and products be assessed for their potential impact on human, animal, and soil health, agrifood systems, and the environment, considering unintended consequences and trade-offs.

instrument: WOAH One Health Strategy
description: Roadmap for embedding One Health within veterinary services, this strategy highlights multisectoral coordination, workforce capacity, and investment needed to manage zoonoses, AMR, food safety, and environmental health—aligned with the Quadripartite One Health Joint Plan of Action. It emphasizes veterinary leadership, national operational tools (e.g., MCM OT), and workforce development as vehicles for holistic health resilience.
governanceRole:
Positions veterinary services as One Health change-agents: It calls for operationalizing coordination mechanisms (e.g., MCM OT) to link veterinary, human and environmental health governance
Focuses on workforce competency: The strategy advances competency-based training, mentorship, and certification for field epidemiologists and veterinary personnel working at spillover hotspots
Promotes integrated surveillance and data systems: WOAH supports WAHIS and WAHIS‑Wild for real-time reporting and cross-sector risk communication and climate-informed surveillance
limitations:
Environment sector engagement remains secondary: While environmental data is referenced, formal partnership with environmental agencies across member countries is inconsistent
Resource constraints hinder implementation: The roadmap depends on investment and capacity that many low- and middle-income countries may struggle to mobilize without external support
Strategy is not enforceable: The strategy's impact relies on alignment with national policy priorities and sustained funding
provisions:
Governance Pillar: Endorses use of the Multisectoral Coordination Mechanisms Operational Tool (MCM OT) to create national One Health coordinating bodies

Workforce Development Pillar: Mandates competency-based training systems for field epidemiology, continuing education, and mentorship across zoonotic and environmental health domains

Surveillance & Information Sharing Pillar: Supports the use of WAHIS and WAHIS‑Wild for joint veterinary–environmental disease monitoring and early warning systems
interlinkages:
One Health Joint Plan of Action
International Health Regulations (IHR)

instrument: Global Action Plan on Climate Change and Health (A78/27)
description: Adopted by WHA decision WHA78(27). A framework aligning health and climate action. It integrates health into climate policies through three areas: leadership and advocacy, evidence and monitoring, and country-level capacity-building. The plan promotes equity, One Health and planetary health approaches, and multisectoral collaboration to strengthen climate‑resilient, low‑carbon health systems and reduce climate-related health risks.
governanceRole:
Equity (pp. 1, 4, 10): Prioritizes vulnerable populations, equity in climate–health financing, and locally led strategies.
One Health integration (p. 10): Promotes intersectoral cooperation linking human, animal, and environmental health in national strategies.
Evidence and monitoring (pp. 7–9): Strengthens research, surveillance, and integrated data systems on climate-sensitive diseases.
Capacity building (pp. 4, 11–14): Provides technical guidance and tools for climate-resilient, low‑carbon health systems.
limitations:
Resource dependence (pp. 4, 13): Implementation relies on mobilizing external funding, creating disparities for low‑income countries.
Coordination complexity (p. 15): Broad multisectoral scope may slow progress due to need for extensive alignment among actors.
Uneven national uptake (p. 10): Actions are nationally determined, risking uneven implementation and impact.
provisions:
Action Area – Leadership, Coordination and Advocacy: Calls on countries to integrate health into national climate plans, mobilize financing, and ensure the health sector participates in climate policy, while WHO coordinates global advocacy and technical support.

Action Area – Evidence and Monitoring: Strengthens research, data, and surveillance on climate-sensitive diseases, and establishes systems to track climate–health risks and the benefits of mitigation and adaptation.

Action Area – Country-Level Action and Capacity-Building: Promotes national strategies for climate-resilient, low-carbon health systems, periodic vulnerability assessments, and support for adaptation planning and finance.

instrument: Global strategy for the prevention and control of high pathogenic avian influenza (2024–2033)
description: Provides a ten-year roadmap to reduce the impacts of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI), especially the H5Nx 2.3.4.4b clade, through a One Health systems approach. It focuses on prevention, protection, and transformation of poultry value chains to mitigate disease, safeguard wildlife and human health, and promote sustainable agrifood systems. The strategy emphasizes risk-based surveillance, integrated animal-wildlife-human data systems, vaccination stewardship, inclusive governance, and sustainable biosecurity. It seeks to build resilient poultry systems while addressing the pandemic potential and ecological disruption caused by HPAI.
governanceRole:
Anchors One Health within operational animal disease control: The strategy embeds One Health into concrete surveillance, vaccination, and biosecurity programs, particularly at the poultry–wildlife–human interface, creating tangible cross-sector pathways for risk reduction​
Strengthens integrated surveillance and response systems: It promotes joint risk-based surveillance across domestic and wild species, facilitates laboratory cooperation, and supports cross-sectoral data sharing through OFFLU and national platforms
Builds institutional capacity through multi-level governance: The strategy establishes global and regional steering committees, intersectoral task forces, and public–private collaboration mechanisms that integrate veterinary, public health, and environmental institutions
limitations:
National-level buy-in and funding are uneven: The strategy assumes countries will prioritize HPAI and invest in One Health capacity, but many LMICs lack dedicated budgets or multisectoral structures, creating gaps in operational delivery and equity
Limited operational inclusion of public health authorities: Despite strong global-level engagement from WHO and public health actors, the strategy offers few mechanisms to systematically embed human health agencies at the country level, especially outside of outbreak response
provisions:
Objective 1, pg. 5: Using a One Health approach to prevent, detect early and rapidly respond is key to reducing the devastating impacts of HPAI outbreaks in domestic and wild animals, and to preventing virus spillover/spillback to wild animals and humans.

Output 3.1, pg. 11: The strategy supports transformation of poultry agrifood systems... using participatory processes involving poultry producers, wildlife ecologists, public health, and consumer groups to promote safe, resilient, and sustainable production aligned with One Health goals.

Output 1.1, pg. 7: Integrated One Health approaches for risk-based surveillance, prevention and response are required to address threats... Surveillance of diseases in wildlife should be integrated into wildlife management and conservation systems.

instrument: Ramsar Resolution IX.23: Highly pathogenic avian influenza and its consequences for wetland and waterbird conservation and wise use
description: Recognizes the ecological, health, and livelihood risks posed by the spread of HPAI (H5N1), rejects lethal control of wild birds and wetland habitat destruction, and calls for coordinated, multisectoral response planning and surveillance. It positions wetland integrity as critical to preventing disease spread and stresses scientific data, international cooperation, and ecosystem-based outbreak management.
governanceRole:
Encourages safe land use of environment with respect to animal health: Culling wild birds and habitat destruction are explicitly rejected as non-“wise use” (¶18).
Calls for integrated contingency planning and data-sharing: Urges countries to develop multisectoral response plans and participate in international data coordination (¶16, ¶19, ¶24).
Promotes cooperation with FAO, WHO, OIE, and CMS: Acknowledges and aligns with existing global HPAI strategies and surveillance platforms (¶7, ¶9, ¶14).
limitations:
Public health and veterinary integration is encouraged but not structurally institutionalized: Success depends on proactive cross-sector participation at the national level.
Scientific uncertainty limits attribution of disease transmission pathways: While migratory birds are acknowledged, trade and poultry vectors are under-emphasized in terms of regulation.
provisions:

¶17–18: Rejects lethal control and habitat destruction as inappropriate and potentially harmful responses.

¶19–20: Supports STRP and Scientific Task Force engagement in knowledge generation and transmission.

¶21–23: Urges capacity-building, contingency planning, and enhanced farming standards.

¶24: Requests the Ramsar Secretariat to coordinate with technical partners to support response and learning.

instrument: Ramsar Resolution VIII.18 Invasive species and wetlands
description: Addresses the growing threat of invasive alien species (IAS) to wetland ecosystems, recognizing their ecological, economic, and health impacts. It calls for national risk assessments, early detection and rapid response, transboundary cooperation, and harmonization of IAS policies with CBD, GISP, and IUCN guidance, including aquatic, terrestrial, and climate-linked invasions.
governanceRole:
Integrates IAS control into national wetland and biodiversity policies: Encourages harmonized legislation and cross-treaty engagement (¶24).
Promotes early detection, risk assessment, and transboundary coordination: Provides a framework for cross-sectoral ecosystem protection (¶16, ¶22).
Includes aquatic and terrestrial IAS in both inland and coastal wetlands: Recognizes hydrological and climate drivers of IAS spread (¶2, ¶21).
limitations:
Implementation relies on national reporting and voluntary alignment with CBD or GISP: Uptake of early warning and control tools is a domestic measure for voluntary uptake (¶4).
Risk of access to information for implementing agencies: Training and capacity-building are encouraged but not resourced (¶26).
provisions:

¶22: Urges cooperation across transboundary wetlands and shared river/coastal systems.

¶26: Supports regional awareness programs (e.g. Africa) and web-based guidance for early detection and management.

instrument: Ramsar Resolution VIII.3: Climate change and wetlands: impacts, adaptation, and mitigation
description: Highlights the dual role of wetlands as both vulnerable to and vital for climate change adaptation and mitigation. It urges Contracting Parties to integrate wetland resilience and carbon storage into national strategies, particularly for peatlands, and to prevent ecological damage from mitigation actions like afforestation or water diversion.
governanceRole:
Identifies wetland degradation as a risk to ecological and human resilience: Links climate vulnerability to waterborne disease, food insecurity, and disaster exposure (¶3, ¶6).
Promotes wetland-based mitigation and adaptation: Supports peatland restoration, watershed protection, and ecosystem-based planning to reduce human and ecosystem vulnerability (¶15–17).
Encourages collaboration with climate science bodies and other MEAs: Advances science-policy coherence across biodiversity, health, and climate frameworks (¶12, ¶22).
limitations:
Limited explicit public health framing: Focus remains on ecosystem protection, with indirect references to human health outcomes.
No operationalization of One Health in surveillance or planning tools: Lacks integration with ministries of health or disease-related monitoring systems.
provisions:

instrument: WOAH Resolution 27: The “One Health” Approach to Address Health Risks at the Animal Human Ecosystem Interface
description:
The resolution promotes integrated One Health governance by linking human, animal, and ecosystem health through collaboration, strong veterinary services, and global partnerships.
The resolution underscores Veterinary Services' role in preventing zoonoses, tackling antimicrobial resistance, and ensuring food safety, emphasizing intersectoral collaboration and integrated approaches. It highlights strengthening Veterinary Services, harmonizing WOAH and WHO standards, incorporating One Health into education, and using rabies control as a One Health model.
governanceRole:
Institutional coordination mechanisms: Promotes the development of cross-sectoral coordination platforms to align veterinary, public health, and environmental actions under a unified One Health approach.
Risk-based policy design: Encourages evidence-informed strategies that integrate ecological and epidemiological data to prevent and control health risks at the animal-human-environment interface.
Monitoring and surveillance systems: Strengthens integrated surveillance efforts across sectors to detect, assess, and respond to emerging zoonotic threats in real time.
limitations:
Fragmented veterinary and environmental integration: Veterinary services often operate independently of environmental health institutions, limiting the resolution’s call for joint action at the animal-human-ecosystem interface.
Challenges for national veterinary services in One Health governance: In many countries, veterinary authorities lack formal mandates or decision-making power in intersectoral platforms, reducing their ability to implement the resolution’s multisectoral goals.
Barriers to integrated surveillance systems: Persistent gaps in interagency data sharing and incompatible surveillance infrastructure across sectors hinder early detection and coordinated response to zoonotic threats.
provisions:
para 4: Recommends that (1) the Director General and the OIE Delegates advocate to governments and regional and international organisations for the fundamental role of Veterinary Services in the protection of animal, human and ecosystem health and the application of “One Health” approaches, and (5) the Director General encourage relevant OIE Reference Centres to further develop the “One Health” concept and approaches to animal disease detection, prevention and control, including economic studies, and further develop and provide capacity building programmes on implementing “One Health” approaches.

para 5: The resolution encourages countries to use the WOAH PVS Tool—a diagnostic framework developed by WOAH that helps countries evaluate the capacity and performance of their national veterinary services, particularly in areas like disease surveillance, emergency response, legislation, and communication.—to identify institutional gaps, enhance veterinary governance, and benchmark progress in implementing cross-sectoral health strategies.

para 8: Recommends that (8) veterinary and medical institutions and faculties worldwide be encouraged to incorporate relevant “One Health” approaches within their undergraduate and postgraduate curricula, including within continuing professional education programmes.

instrument: Conference Resolution 4/2015: Antimicrobial Resistance
description: Conference Resolution 4/2015 commits FAO to a central role in the global response to antimicrobial resistance, emphasizing a One Health approach that links agriculture, food systems, and public health. It endorses FAO’s action plan on AMR, urges Member States to develop national AMR strategies covering animal, plant, and environmental health, and calls for multisectoral cooperation with WHO and OIE (now WOAH). The resolution also directs FAO to integrate AMR into its normative work, surveillance systems, capacity building, and technical support, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.
governanceRole:
Institutional anchoring of AMR within FAO’s mandate: Gives FAO a clear leadership role on AMR in food, agriculture, and the environment, reinforcing its legitimacy in One Health coordination.
Support for multisectoral national action plans: Encourages Members to develop and implement cross-sectoral AMR strategies, promoting whole-of-government approaches.
Integration of AMR into food safety and surveillance systems: Links AMR to Codex, veterinary services, and national monitoring frameworks, enabling aligned standards and data systems.
limitations:
Limited operational detail on environmental implementation: Acknowledges environmental drivers of AMR but lacks concrete mechanisms or targets for environmental sector engagement.
Voluntary nature weakens accountability: Encourages action but does not require binding commitments, leaving implementation uneven across Member States.
Narrow focus on food and agriculture sectors: Does not fully address integration with human health systems, limiting its reach as a truly unified One Health instrument.
provisions:

instrument: Conference Resolution 6/2019: Antimicrobial Resistance
description: Resolution 6/2019 reaffirms FAO’s leadership role in addressing AMR through a One Health approach, and calls for coordination across sectors and agencies. It endorses ongoing collaboration with WHO, WOAH, and UNEP; urges Members to strengthen evidence, surveillance, and prudent antimicrobial use in agriculture and the environment; and emphasizes support for developing countries and regular reporting on AMR progress.
governanceRole:
Endorses the Tripartite coordination framework: The resolution formally recognizes the expanded collaboration between FAO, WHO, WOAH, and notes UNEP workplan on AMR, as well as other relevant international organizations, by strengthening global governance of AMR by embedding environmental dimensions alongside human and animal health.
Aligns FAO’s AMR work with the WHO Global Action Plan: By calling for coordinated implementation and shared progress reporting among agencies, it fosters consistency and coherence across sectors—key to operationalizing One Health at global and national levels.
Prioritizes technical support and equity for low- and middle-income countries: The resolution highlights the need for capacity building, access to diagnostics, vaccines, surveillance infrastructure, and prudent use policies in agriculture and food systems—empowering LMICs to participate fully in One Health-aligned AMR responses.

Limited operational detail on environmental integration: the resolution lacks clarity on how environmental surveillance, waste management, and pollution control will be operationalized or resourced.

instrument: Resolution 14: OIE's Engagement in the One Health Global Effort to Control Antimicrobial Resistance
description: The resolution strengthens global coordination to tackle antimicrobial resistance (AMR) through a One Health approach, focusing on international collaboration, national action plans, and sustainable investments in AMR efforts. Key elements include Coordination through the Tripartite, support for National Action Plans, monitoring progress, resource mobilization via the AMR Multi-Partner Trust Fund, strengthening OIE’s role, and regular updates on AMR progress.
governanceRole:
Promotion of responsible antimicrobial stewardship: Drives national and global efforts to optimize antimicrobial use in animals, aligning veterinary practice with public health and environmental sustainability goals.
Surveillance and data harmonization across sectors: Supports the development of integrated AMR surveillance systems, especially through WOAH’s global database (ANIMUSE), to improve data sharing and coordination across human, animal, and environmental sectors.
Capacity building in veterinary governance: Strengthens veterinary systems through training, guidance, and policy support to implement AMR national action plans and engage effectively in One Health governance structures.
limitations:
Limited regulation of antimicrobial use in animal sectors: Many countries lack comprehensive legal frameworks to govern the use of antimicrobials in food-producing animals, undermining efforts to reduce misuse and overuse that fuel resistance.
Inconsistent AMR surveillance and reporting systems: Surveillance of antimicrobial resistance in animals is often fragmented or absent, and disparities in reporting to global systems like ANIMUSE hinder data-driven, cross-sectoral responses.
Insufficient veterinary capacity for stewardship and enforcement: Veterinary services in several Member Countries lack the technical expertise, infrastructure, or political authority to implement AMR stewardship programs or enforce prudent-use guidelines effectively.
provisions:
Res. 14, para 3: The resolution reaffirms WOAH’s commitment to assist Member Countries in developing and implementing national AMR action plans that align with the Global Action Plan on AMR and apply a One Health lens across sectors.

Res. 14, para 4: It urges Members to collect and report data on antimicrobial use in animals through WOAH’s global ANIMUSE system, and promotes harmonization of surveillance methodologies to enhance data comparability and global monitoring.

Res. 14, end: The resolution encourages Members to improve legislation and governance around antimicrobial access and usage in animals, including efforts to eliminate non-therapeutic use and promote responsible veterinary practices through a permanent working group

Res. 14, para 9: It urges contributions to the WOAH Partner Fund to enable low- and middle-income countries to implement national AMR plans, strengthen veterinary services, and access technical support—helping to translate guidance into action.
interlinkages:
WHO Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance
WOAH Strategy on Antimicrobial Resistance
Codex Code of Practice to Minimize and Contain Foodborne AMR (CXC 61-2005, revised 2021)

instrument: WHA 73.5: Strengthening efforts on food safety
description: The resolution reaffirms food safety as a core component of public health and sustainable development. Calls on Member States to strengthen national food safety systems through a One Health approach, cross-sector collaboration, and integration with health, agriculture, trade, and environment policies. Emphasizes investment in regulatory systems, surveillance, laboratory capacity, emergency response, and participation in Codex and INFOSAN. Requests WHO to update the global food safety strategy in coordination with FAO to address emerging challenges and new technologies.
governanceRole:
Promotes a One Health approach to food safety through cross-sector collaboration across health, agriculture, trade, and environment. Encourages investment, innovation, and data sharing to enhance national systems and equity across sectors.
Calls for health-in-all-policies approach to ensure adequate collaboration to ensure sustainability, availability, and access to safe and nutritious food for all populations
Advocates for collaboration with other IOs: Refers to the need to increase the use of Codex standards and calls for collaboration between the WHO and FAO
limitations: Focus remains largely on national government action, with less explicit integration of environmental sectors or community participation. Implementation may vary due to uneven national capacities and resources.
provisions:
Preamble: Underlining that a One Health approach to food safety includes managing food safety risks along the entire food and feed chain; and recognizing that the interconnection between food safety and human, animal, plant and environmental health is necessary for the protection of human life and health and food safety, and that it should be pursued in the vision and strategic objectives of WHO.

OP 1(3): Urges Member States to strengthen cross-sector collaboration, using a health-in-all-policies approach, and to apply a One Health approach to promote the sustainability and availability of, and access to, safe, sufficient and nutritious food for all populations, while recognizing the importance of affordability.
interlinkages:
Codex General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995, Revised 2023)
General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969, Revised 2022)
WTO Agreement on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS)

instrument: WHA 74.7: Strengthening WHO preparedness for and response to health emergencies
description: WHA 74.7 establishes a comprehensive roadmap for strengthening WHO and Member State capacities to prepare for and respond to health emergencies. It calls for enhanced One Health collaboration, improved surveillance, equitable access to health tools, and more effective governance. It also requests WHO to support countries with technical guidance, develop new emergency alert levels, and strengthen cross-sectoral early warning systems.
governanceRole:
Institutionalized One Health coordination at global level: Directs WHO to work with FAO, OIE (WOAH), and UNEP to develop a joint One Health strategy and workplan, formalizing cross-agency collaboration to prevent, detect, and respond to zoonotic outbreaks and health emergencies
Integrated early warning and surveillance systems across sectors: Calls for the strengthening of reporting mechanisms, notably the Global Early Warning System (GLEWS), and improvement of communication between human, animal, and environmental surveillance networks
Support for country-led, multisectoral emergency preparedness: Reinforces WHO’s role in supporting Member States to adopt all-hazard, multisectoral preparedness systems, grounded in the IHR (2005) and inclusive of One Health frameworks for detection and response
limitations:
Human health remains the dominant frame of reference: Despite referencing One Health, the resolution centers health emergencies within human health systems, limiting integration of environmental and animal health perspectives
One Health commitments lack operational specificity: Mandates coordination between WHO and FAO, OIE, and UNEP, but provides little detail on implementation mechanisms, accountability, or resourcing.
Member State-driven design may marginalize non-state expertise: The WHO-led reform processes focus on Member States, potentially sidelining the voices of local communities, Indigenous knowledge holders, and frontline environmental actors critical to One Health
provisions:
OP 7(3): Urges Member States to adopt an all-hazard, multisectoral, coordinated approach in preparedness for health emergencies, recognizing the links between human, animal and environmental health and the need for a One Health approach

OP 8, 9, 10: Requests the [DG], as soon as practicably possible and in consultation with Member States: … (8) to review and strengthen or reform, as applicable, existing tripartite reporting mechanisms, such as the Global Early Warning System for Major Animal Diseases (GLEWS), improving communication and information exchange across existing surveillance networks across the One Health sectors; (9) to build on and strengthen the existing cooperation between WHO, FAO, OIE and UNEP to develop options, for consideration by their respective governing bodies, including establishing a common strategy on One Health, including a joint workplan on One Health to improve prevention, monitoring, detection, control and containment of zoonotic disease outbreaks; (10) to report on efforts to accumulate expertise on and raise visibility of One Health issues with a specific focus on zoonoses, including from wildlife, through the work of the One Health High Level Expert Panel ….

OP 8(2): CALLS ON international actors, partners, civil society and the private sector to strengthen partnerships, global coordination and cooperation in response to infectious diseases based on lessons learned from the COVID-19 pandemic and previous public health emergencies of international concern and fostering a One Health, whole-of-society and health systems strengthening approach, including between WHO and relevant multilateral organizations, including the signatory agencies of the global action plan for healthy lives and well-being for all …
interlinkages:
International Health Regulations
WHO Pandemic Agreement
PIP Framework

instrument: UNEA Resolultion 5/6: Biodiversity and Health
description: This resolution formally recognizes the interlinkages between biodiversity, ecosystem health, and human well-being. It emphasizes the role of One Health in preventing pandemics, supports coordinated action on biodiversity loss and environmental drivers of disease, and encourages integration of biodiversity-health considerations across national and international policies.
governanceRole:
Promotes capacity building and financing for LMICs: Encourages international cooperation and funding for health–environment programs in vulnerable settings (OP 9, OP 12)
Aligns biodiversity protection with zoonotic disease prevention: Connects restoration, conservation, and sustainable use to reduced disease emergence risk (OP 2, OP 8)
Highlights health risks in the event of adverse events: Frames the need for monitoring and surveillance within the context of spillover events
limitations:
Health sector engagement is advisory, not structural: While supportive, the resolution does not require engagement or collaboration with health ministries or health surveillance systems in biodiversity governance, which would improve effective implementation
No measurable benchmarks or accountability indicators: The resolution lacks outcome metrics to track biodiversity–health integration progress
provisions:
OP 2: Encourages countries to mainstream biodiversity-health linkages in national programs and policies.

OP 5: Encourages Member States to reduce zoonotic spillover and prevent pandemics through sustainable use and biodiversity restoration.

OP 12: Calls on international partners to support developing countries with capacity building and financing for biodiversity-health priorities.

OP 13: Highlights antimicrobial resistance as a priority issue tied to environmental transmission and pollution

instrument: WHA 75.13: Global strategy on infection prevention and control
description: WHA 75.13 mandates the development of a global strategy on infection prevention and control (IPC) to strengthen health systems and reduce the burden of healthcare-associated infections and antimicrobial resistance. It urges Member States to implement and monitor IPC programs across all levels of care, incorporate a One Health approach, and align efforts with existing frameworks on AMR, WASH, and health emergencies. It also tasks WHO with creating a measurable action plan through 2030, supported by ongoing technical guidance and biennial progress reporting.
governanceRole:
Integration of IPC with AMR, WASH, and emergency response systems: Calls for IPC programs to be aligned with national strategies on antimicrobial resistance, water and sanitation, and health emergencies, creating cross-sectoral entry points for One Health coordination.
Workforce development and education: Emphasizes creating IPC-specific career pathways, mandates, and accredited education programs—enabling health systems to build skilled, accountable IPC leadership across settings.
Measurable, system-wide implementation and monitoring: Establishes a framework for national and facility-level IPC implementation, monitored through WHO core components and a forthcoming action plan with 2030 targets—creating institutional accountability for One Health-aligned infection control.
limitations:
Weak IPC presence outside hospitals: When infection control is narrowly confined to hospitals, it disrupts One Health-aligned governance by excluding the community, long-term care, and home-based sectors, where risks related to zoonoses, environmental exposures, and antimicrobial misuse can also arise. This undermines system-wide resilience and One Health coordination.
Fragmented HAI and AMR data: The lack of integrated, multilevel monitoring of healthcare-associated infections and resistance patterns prevents public health, veterinary, and environmental authorities from coordinating early responses
IPC professionals lack structural authority to drive multisectoral alignment: Without defined mandates and recognition, IPC leads cannot participate meaningfully in national or multisectoral governance platforms, which limits their ability to contribute to One Health-aligned planning on AMR, emergency response, or health facility design.
provisions:
OP3, Section 1: Calls on Member States: … (3) to take steps to support and/or to ensure that science-based functional infection prevention and control programmes exist – for both community-acquired and health care-associated infections, taking into account the One Health approach – are implemented, monitored and updated at national, subnational, and/or facility levels, as appropriate to national contexts and in line with WHO’s core components of such programmes...

OP6, Section 1: Calls on Member States… to ensure that sustainable IPC, water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructures and resources are in place and utilized across all healthcare facilities, including in primary healthcare, home and community-based settings, and long-term care…

OP2, Section 2: Requests the Director-General… to translate this global strategy… into an action plan for infection prevention and control, including a framework for tracking progress with clear measurable targets to be achieved by 2030
interlinkages: WHO Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance

instrument: WHA 76.17: The impact of chemicals, waste and pollution on human health
description: The resolution calls upon Member States to strengthen their commitments to the WHO Global Strategy on Health, Environment, and Climate in order to address the risk of plastics, hazardous chemicals, and waste to health by continuing to support cross-sectoral policy engagement on these topics to minmize human harm and understand the impacts of chemical production.
governanceRole:
Strengthening of surveillance, biomonitoring, and poison control systems The resolution and DG report both emphasize the need to build national capacity in biomonitoring, poison centres, and surveillance of chemical exposures, including human biomonitoring systems and early warning networks. This supports a One Health model of integrated risk detection across sectors​.
Institutionalization of multisectoral governance through the Global Framework on Chemicals: The DG report notes that the newly adopted Global Framework on Chemicals promotes integrated legal and institutional mechanisms across health, environment, labor, and agriculture sectors.
Alignment of chemical and pollution policy with broader health goals: The resolution enables the integration of environmental health risks into core public health priorities, encouraging health systems to account for pollution as a key social determinant
limitations:
Fragmented governance across sectors managing chemicals and waste: The report highlights a lack of coherent legal and institutional structures that link health with environmental, labor, and agricultural agencies, limiting coordinated action​
Weak national systems for biomonitoring and poison control: Many countries lack functioning poison centres and systems to track chemical exposures in humans, undermining early detection and response to environmental health threats
Limited health sector engagement in pollution policy: Despite high disease burdens, health ministries often play a marginal role in environmental and waste governance, especially in implementing frameworks like the Global Framework on Chemicals
provisions:
WHA76.17, para 1: Urges Member States to take the impact of chemicals, waste and pollution on human health into account in relevant national, regional and international policies, plans and processes, including those related to chemicals and waste, air and water quality, and food safety”

WHA76.17, para 4: Requests the Director General: (1) to publish a report, incorporating science and risk based-assessments and conclusions on the human health implications of chemicals, waste and pollution as well as reporting on existing data gaps, including from a One Health approach, ensuring data disaggregation by sex, age, disability and any other relevant factor, that takes into account persistent and bio accumulative and persistent and mobile substances, as well as substances that are carcinogenic, mutagenic or reprotoxic, neurotoxic, immunotoxin or harmful to cardiovascular, respiratory and other organ systems, or endocrine disruptors; (2) in consultation with other One Health Quadripartite members, to further develop research on the linkages among human and animal health and the environment, such as in the case of chemicals, waste and pollution
interlinkages:
Basel Convention
Rotterdam Convention
Stockholm Convention
Minamata Convention

instrument: CMS Resolution 12.6: Wildlife health & migratory species
description: Affirms the interdependence of wildlife, human, and ecosystem health, emphasizing disease prevention, non-infectious threats (e.g., pollution, stress), and the role of healthy ecosystems in fostering resilience. It calls for One Health-based governance, non-lethal and science-based responses, and cross-sector collaboration to address wildlife health holistically.
governanceRole:
Recognizes environmental drivers of wildlife disease beyond pathogens: Includes stressors like climate disruption, toxins, and undernutrition (Preamble, §5).
Advocates for upstream, non-lethal management strategies: Encourages ecosystem restoration and preventive planning rather than reactive culling or habitat destruction.
Builds continuity with prior wildlife-health resolutions and international guidance: Updates and consolidates previous resolutions (8.27, 9.8, 10.22), reinforcing long-term institutional memory
limitations:
Absence of a formal implementation mechanism or reporting framework: No compliance measures or timelines included.
Health sector roles are supportive rather than institutionalized: While the resolution is cross-sectoral, national health ministries are not mandated participants.
Data limitations in many countries undermine actionability: Acknowledged need for increased research, surveillance, and coordination, especially in the Global South
provisions:
Preamble: Recognizes the full suite of drivers of wildlife disease, including infectious, toxicological, nutritional, and climate-related causes.

§2: Emphasizes that ecosystem health determines resilience across species and sectors.

§4: Reiterates CMS’s commitment to non-lethal, science-based responses aligned with FAO, WOAH, Ramsar, and CBD mandates.

§5: Links wildlife health deterioration to broader conservation and One Health goals, especially for migratory species.
interlinkages:
Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS)
Ramsar Convention
International Health Regulations

instrument: CMS Resolution 14/18: Avian influenza
description: Addresses the threat of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) to migratory birds, ecosystems, livestock, and human health. It outlines a One Health approach for outbreak response, coordination across sectors, ecosystem protection, and prevention of zoonotic spillover, while rejecting culling and habitat destruction as response strategies.
governanceRole:
Formally applies a One Health lens to HPAI outbreak preparedness and response: Calls for virological, ecological, and epidemiological integration in planning and monitoring (¶1c, ¶4).
Rejects harmful wildlife control and habitat destruction policies: Aligns with FAO/WOAH/Ramsar guidance against lethal responses (¶2).
Establishes a conservation-driven surveillance model: Encourages monitoring, early warning, and wildlife data-sharing across sectors and countries (¶4, ¶5, ¶7)
limitations:
funding: Implementation is voluntary and contingent on national and donor support (¶6).
Human health agencies are supporting actors but not required implementers: WHO is mentioned, but national health systems are not institutionally mandated within the resolution.
Limited guidance on integrating surveillance with public health systems: Wildlife-focused monitoring is strong, but human disease surveillance linkages are underdeveloped
provisions:
¶1: Calls for national wildlife HPAI contingency plans, cross-sectoral planning, and integrated outbreak response.

¶2: Requests that responses avoid culling, habitat destruction, and environmentally harmful measures.

¶3: Recommends multisectoral measures to prevent spillover and manage high-risk trade, farming, and wetland use.

¶4: Supports surveillance, data-sharing, and research to assess HPAI impacts on wild bird populations.

¶6: Urges donor support for Task Force recommendations; ¶7 requests integration into National Reports and future CoP reviews
interlinkages:
Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS)
Ramsar Convention
International Health Regulations
Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework
Terrestrial Animal Health Code

instrument: Resolution Conf. 10.21 (Rev. CoP19): Transport of live specimens
description: Provides guidelines for the humane and health-conscious transport of live CITES-listed animals and plants. It encourages Parties to adopt IATA transport standards, minimize stress and mortality in transit, and incorporate health safeguards to reduce animal injury, cruelty, and disease transmission risk during trade. It supports collaboration with IATA, WOAH, IPPC, and other standard-setting bodies.
governanceRole:
Codifies health and welfare safeguards in international wildlife logistics: Integrates IATA and CITES transport standards into national permitting and enforcement processes (Rec. 2a, 2g, 6).
Recognizes disease risks linked to transport-induced stress and improper handling: Addresses transport-related immunosuppression and high-mortality shipments as threats to animal health and zoonotic risk (Preamble ¶8, Rec. 3d).
Encourages collaboration with veterinary and scientific experts: Recommends engagement of NGOs and standard-setting bodies for capacity-building (Rec. 5)
limitations:
Focus remains on species conservation and humane treatment rather than integrated disease surveillance: No direct mechanisms link transport compliance with public health monitoring.
Implementation varies based on national capacity and regulatory frameworks: Reliant on Parties’ willingness and ability to legislate and enforce IATA/CITES guidelines.
Non-binding nature may limit accountability: While widely respected, adoption of recommendations is voluntary and often lacks resourced follow-up
provisions:
Preamble ¶8: Acknowledges that transport stress may suppress immunity and increase infectious disease risk.

Rec. 2(a, g, h): Recommends that Parties use IATA standards and examine shipments at transfer points for welfare and health compliance.

Rec. 3(d): Directs Parties to investigate high-mortality shipments and issue recommendations to reduce recurrence.

Rec. 5: Invites NGOs with veterinary and transport expertise to assist Parties in effective implementation.

Rec. 6: Encourages application of IATA and CITES guidelines in domestic legs of international trade.
interlinkages: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES)

instrument: Resolution Conf. 13.10 (Rev. CoP14): Trade in invasive alien species
description: Acknowledges that international trade in live animals and plants can contribute to the spread of invasive alien species (IAS), and recommends that Parties incorporate IAS risk considerations into CITES permitting processes. It encourages collaboration between CITES and the CBD to address IAS risks within trade regulation.
governanceRole:
Integrates IAS prevention into international trade governance: Encourages national legislation to consider the biosecurity and ecological risks of species in commercial trade (Rec. 1a).
Promotes risk consultation between importing and exporting states: Recommends bilateral communication to avoid unintended introductions (Rec. 1b).
Strengthens cooperation between CITES and CBD: Recognizes the need for synergy between biodiversity conservation and invasive species regulation (Rec. 1c).
limitations:
No explicit integration of public health surveillance or veterinary sectors: Focuses on ecological risk, without specific consideration of zoonotic or agricultural disease vectors.
Relies on national capacity to assess and regulate risk: Effectiveness depends on whether domestic authorities have tools and mandates to manage IAS in trade.
provisions:
Rec. 1(a): Recommends Parties consider IAS risks in domestic legislation on trade in live specimens.

Rec. 1(b): Advises exporters to consult with importers about domestic IAS regulations.

Rec. 1(c): Calls for cooperation and synergy between CITES and CBD on alien species introductions.
interlinkages:
Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES)
Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
WTO Agreement on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS)
